Bernard Johnathan Denson writes:

The hundreds of students who have passed through St. Bernard Prep School have many common experiences that will forever bind them together. But for those of us who lived in the Boys’ Dorm from 1985 – 2011, perhaps no single thing could epitomize what it meant to be a Bernardian more than Al Moelter: As Dorm Director for those 26 years, he was a permanent fixture in our lives that provided discipline, demanded integrity, and—whether we would admit it at the time, or not—shaped us into the men we are today. The Mr. Moelter stories that could—and surely will—be told by SBP alumni are inexhaustible: From having to “hit the floor,” to that jerk in your stomach when he had just yelled your name up the stairwell; from room inspections, to pizza parties; and who could forget his signature pocket protector, or the feeling that you had to add the word “sir” to the end of any sentence addressed to him? Mr. Al Moelter is truly nothing short of legendary, and he will live on in the memories of those who knew him. There are so many of us in the St. Bernard family who wish that the era of Al and Dorothy Moelter could have lasted forever; they were amazing. Thank you so much, Mr. Moelter, for everything you did for all of us!

FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

A reflection by one of the monks of St. Bernard Abbey:

On this First Sunday of Advent and the first Sunday of the new liturgical year, Mother Church begins the four weeks of preparation leading to the coming feast of Christmas not by focusing on the Nativity, nor John the Baptist’s “Prepare the way for the Lord,” nor the Archangel Gabriel’s proclamation to the Virgin Mary, nor any event concerning the birth of Christ at Bethlehem. 

Rather, Advent begins with readings and propers concentrated on hope in the future coming of Christ. This emphasis places us in the shoes of the Hebrew people of 2,000 years ago, for whom the coming of the Messiah was not a historical fact of the distant past, but instead a hope for what would come. We, the people of God living today in the year 2012, also claim to be awaiting his coming—his second coming, his return in glory at the end of days.

We, as individual members of the Church, make this claim in the face of a post-modern and post-Christian world that has declared with Nietzsche, “God is dead.” As Advent begins, we acclaim to this world that Jesus Christ is not just another figure from the history books. We acclaim that he is God, the living God, the God who made all things, who has come among us bringing salvation and who will indeed come again. We profess that he is the most real and most alive thing there is. 

In the celebration of the First Sunday of Advent, the liturgy invites us to oppose mainstream society and acknowledge the fact that we desperately need God. Without him we would not exist, without him we would perish, and without him we would have no hope. The text for this Sunday’s Introit, Responsorial Psalm, and Offertory comes from the Twenty-Fifth Psalm: A prayer of hopeful trust in the Lord. This Advent, as we prepare to celebrate Christ’s first coming and contemplate his second, let us say with the psalmist, “O my God, I trust in you…for you are the God of my salvation. I have hoped in you all day long.”

THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT: GAUDETE SUNDAY

This Sunday is known by the first word of its proper introit, "gaudete," which means "rejoice."  The text comes from St. Paul's letter to the Philippians: "Rejoice in the Lord always.  I shall say it again: rejoice!"  We rejoice because the waiting of Advent is half-way over; the coming of the Lord is near.  The color of vestments used on this Sunday reflects the excitement of joy breaking through the darkness of our anticipation:  Advent's normal color of violet is replaced by lighter colored rose vestments (one of St. Bernard Abbey's is pictured here).

From a sermon on this Sunday's Gospel by St. Augustine:

"John is the voice, but the Lord is the Word who was in the beginning. John is the voice that lasts for a time; from the beginning Christ is the Word who lives for ever. Take away the word, the meaning, and what is the voice? Where there is no understanding, there is only a meaningless sound. The voice without the word strikes the ear but does not build up the heart....What does 'prepare the way' mean, if not 'pray well'? What does 'prepare the way' mean, if not 'be humble in your thoughts'? We should take our lesson from John the Baptist. He is thought to be the Christ; he declares he is not what they think. He does not take advantage of their mistake to further his own glory.  If he had said, 'I am the Christ,' you can imagine how readily he would have been believed, since they believed he was the Christ even before he spoke. But he did not say it; he acknowledged what he was. He pointed out clearly who he was; he humbled himself.  He saw where his salvation lay. He understood that he was a lamp, and his fear was that it might be blown out by the wind of pride.

The "O Antiphons" begin today:

"The seven antiphons to the Magnificat in the ferial Office of the seven days preceeding the vigil of Christmas; so called because all begin with the interjection "O". Their opening words are: (1) "O Sapientia", (2) "O Adonai", (3) "O Radix Jesse", (4) "O Clavis David", (5) "O Oriens", (6) "O Rex Gentium", (7) "O Emmanuel". Addressed to Christ under one or other of His Scriptural titles, they conclude with a distinct petition to the coming Lord (e.g.: "O Wisdom … come and teach us the way of prudence"; "O Adonai … come and redeem us by thy outstretched arm"; "O Key of David … come and lead from prison the captive sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death" etc.). Couched in a poetic and Scriptural phraseology they constitute a notable feature of the Advent Offices."

SEPTEMBER 29, THE 122ND ANNIVERSARY OF THE FOUNDING OF ST. BERNARD ABBEY:

In the 1870s monks from Saint Vincent Archabbey (Latrobe, PA) were sent to Northern Alabama to serve the needs of the Catholics in that area.  On this day--September 29--in 1891, those monks gathered in the sacristy of Sacred Heart Church in Cullman to elect their first abbot, and thereby establish Saint Bernard Abbey.

Abbot Benedict Menges, O.S.B., was unanimously chosen as the founding abbot of the new community. The following months saw both Abbot Benedict’s abbatial blessing, and the erection of the first physical structures of Saint Bernard Abbey on a property the monks bought just East of town.

So, Happy Birthday to us!

Today, the Memorial of St. Jerome, Br. Leo Borelli, O.S.B., will be formally installed as a hermit by the Right Reverend Abbot Cletus Meagher, O.S.B., in the presence of the monastic community after a procession to his new hermitage following our Conventual Mass.

A monk becoming a hermit is a rarity, but St. Benedict sees it as the highest form of monastic life, for which very few are strong enough: 

"... there are the anchorites or hermits, who have come through the test of living in a monastery for a long time, and have passed beyond the first fervor of monastic life.  Thanks to the help and guidance of many, they are now trained to fight against the devil.  They have built up their strength and go from the battle line in the ranks of their brothers to the single combat of the desert.  Self-reliant now, without the support of another, they are ready with God's help to grapple single-handed with the vices of body and mind..." (RB 1:3-5)

Let us pray for Br. Leo!

November 27, 1931 – October 22, 2013

It is with heavy hearts that the Monks of Saint Bernard Abbey announce the death of our confrere, Brother André Couture.  Brother André was born in 1931 in Gravelbourg, Saskatchewan, Canada.  After serving in the U.S. Armed Forces, he became an American citizen.  He professed vows as a Benedictine monk at St. Leo Abbey, Florida, on February 20, 1984, and later transferred his stability to St. Bernard.  For years, he faithfully served as Guestmaster of the Abbey.  He died today at Cullman Regional Medical Center, having received the Sacrament of Anointing.

Eternal rest, grant unto him O Lord and let perpetual light shine upon him.  May his soul and the souls of all the faithful departed, through the mercy of God, rest in peace.  Amen.

ASH WEDNESDAY:
As our Lord spent forty days of fasting and prayer in the wilderness, facing the Evil One, in preparation for his public ministry, which would end in his passion and resurrection, let us likewise commence these forty days of spiritual preparation for the celebration of the mystery of our salvation at Easter.

From the Rule of St. Benedict
"The life of a monk ought to be a continuous Lent. Since few, however, have the strength for this, we urge the entire community during these days of Lent to keep its manner of life most pure and to wash away in this holy season the negligences of other times. This we can do in a fitting manner by refusing to indulge evil habits and by devoting ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, to compunction of heart and self-denial. During these days, therefore, we will add to the usual measure of our service something by way of private prayer and abstinence from food or drink, so that each of us will have something above the assigned measure to offer God of his own will with the joy of the Holy Spirit. In other words, let each one deny himself some food, drink, sleep, needless talking and idle jesting, and look forward to holy Easter with joy and spiritual longing."

Grant, O Lord, that we may begin with holy fasting this campaign of Christian service, so that, as we take up battle against spiritual evils, we may be armed with weapons of self-restraint. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever.  Amen.

Gospel of the Day

What sort of soil is your heart made of?

Jesus said to his disciples:
“Hear the parable of the sower.
The seed sown on the path is the one who hears the word of the Kingdom
without understanding it,
and the Evil One comes and steals away
what was sown in his heart.
The seed sown on rocky ground
is the one who hears the word and receives it at once with joy.
But he has no root and lasts only for a time.
When some tribulation or persecution comes because of the word,
he immediately falls away.
The seed sown among thorns is the one who hears the word,
but then worldly anxiety and the lure of riches choke the word
and it bears no fruit.
But the seed sown on rich soil
is the one who hears the word and understands it,
who indeed bears fruit and yields a hundred or sixty or thirtyfold.”

Tonight, at Vespers (evening prayer), the Church begins the "O Antiphons," which are sung leading up to Christmas, from December 17-23. These seven ancient antiphons, which invoke the coming Messiah under a different title each evening, are the basis for the verses of the well-known hymn "O Come Emmanuel."
The seven antiphons, each beginning with a different prophetic title are:
O SAPIENTIA (O WISDOM, coming forth from the mouth of the Most High, reaching from one end to the other, mightily and sweetly ordering all things: Come and teach us the way of prudence.)
O ADONAI (O LORD, and leader of the House of Israel, who appeared to Moses in the fire of the burning bush and gave him the law on Sinai: Come and redeem us with an outstretched arm.)
O RADIX JESSE (O ROOT OF JESSE standing as a sign among the peoples; before you kings will shut their mouths, to you the nations will make their prayer: Come and deliver us, and delay no longer.)
O CLAVIS DAVID (O KEY OF DAVID and sceptre of the House of Israel; you open and no one can shut; you shut and no one can open: Come and lead the prisoners from the prison house, those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death.)
O ORIENS (O MORNING STAR, splendour of light eternal and sun of righteousness: Come and enlighten those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death.)
O REX GENTIUM (O KING OF NATIONS, and their desire, the cornerstone making both one: Come and save the human race, which you fashioned from clay.)
O EMMANUEL (O EMMANUEL, our king and our lawgiver, the hope of the nations and their Saviour: Come and save us, O Lord our God.)
Interestingly, when these antiphons are completed, on the evening of December 23, one can look back on what has been sung over the last seven days, taking the first letter of each title in reverse order (from Emmanuel to Sapientia) and find a new insight in the word formed: ERO CRAS, Latin for "tomorrow I will be." And indeed, the next night, the Universal Church will gather to celebrate the birth of the Savior.
You can listen to all seven here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8ngcQDQfhlA&list=PLM_BPPe3btzjYhja2ufL8ffepQLsk3KQ8

The Journey Of The Magi by TS Eliot

'A cold coming we had of it,
Just the worst time of the year
For a journey, and such a long journey:
The ways deep and the weather sharp,
The very dead of winter.'
And the camels galled, sorefooted, refractory,
Lying down in the melting snow.
There were times we regretted
The summer palaces on slopes, the terraces,
And the silken girls bringing sherbet.
Then the camel men cursing and grumbling
and running away, and wanting their liquor and women,
And the night-fires going out, and the lack of shelters,
And the cities hostile and the towns unfriendly
And the villages dirty and charging high prices:
A hard time we had of it.
At the end we preferred to travel all night,
Sleeping in snatches,
With the voices singing in our ears, saying
That this was all folly.

Then at dawn we came down to a temperate valley,
Wet, below the snow line, smelling of vegetation;
With a running stream and a water-mill beating the darkness,
And three trees on the low sky,
And an old white horse galloped away in the meadow.
Then we came to a tavern with vine-leaves over the lintel,
Six hands at an open door dicing for pieces of silver,
And feet kiking the empty wine-skins.
But there was no information, and so we continued
And arriving at evening, not a moment too soon
Finding the place; it was (you might say) satisfactory.

All this was a long time ago, I remember,
And I would do it again, but set down
This set down
This: were we led all that way for
Birth or Death? There was a Birth, certainly
We had evidence and no doubt. I had seen birth and death,
But had thought they were different; this Birth was
Hard and bitter agony for us, like Death, our death.
We returned to our places, these Kingdoms,
But no longer at ease here, in the old dispensation,
With an alien people clutching their gods.
I should be glad of another death.

In the monastic tradition, deceased monks are remembered at supper on the anniversary of their death. A "death notice" is read, recounting the life of the monk. See here the death notice for:

Brother Anselm Christopher Kuehler, O.S.B.
March 4, 1960 – January 25, 2016

On the fourth day of March 1960, Christopher Michael Kuehler was born the second child of Hank Kuehler and Carol Hallaran Kuehler at Dallas, Texas.  That same month he was washed in the baptismal waters at Mary Immaculate Church, Dallas, and in the context of a loving and faithful family began his life’s relentless endeavor to follow Christ.  Eventually, the family would grow to be a large one, with seven children in all.  By the time young Christopher was in the fourth grade he was making plans to become a priest, even constructing an altar for himself to “say Mass” and studying arduously to learn the priests’ Latin prayers just as the vernacular translation was being implemented, which upset him after all of his hard work.  

In 1971, the family moved from Dallas to Richmond, Virginia.  The following year, the family was struck by tragedy in the death of Christopher’s four-year-old sister, Mary, an event which would become a defining point in his life.  Despite this tribulation, the Richmond years would prove to be formative and happy times for Christopher.  The baby of the family, Joe, was born, and Christopher eventually transferred from public school to Benedictine Military Institute.  About this experience, he would later write, “I no longer had to explain what being Catholic was or what being a priest meant … I could periodically participate in the Divine Office with the monks.  Life was indeed good.”  

He was disappointed to learn he would not be able to finish at Benedictine, as his father was assuming a new job in Hunstsville, Alabama.  There, Christopher became involved in his parish and graduated from Hunstville High School in 1978.  Having discussed the possibility of a priestly vocation with the diocese, he enrolled as a college seminarian at the University of Dallas, where he became acquainted with the Cistercian monks.  He earned his undergraduate degree in English in 1982, and though he decided to not enter the seminary’s theologate, he continued to be open to the the priesthood and completed the course work for a master’s degree in theology.  In the spring of 1985, he was hired as an assistant to the director of the University of Dallas’s Rome Campus, and thus spent ten months living in Rome, Italy, and travelling in various other parts of Europe.  

Spanning a successful and esteemed educational career of twenty-four years, Mr. Kuehler—as he was called—taught theology and English, and coached cross country at Bishop Lynch High School in Dallas, Texas; Saint Ann’s School in Decatur, Alabama; and Saint Bernard Preparatory School in Cullman, Alabama.  He had discovered something he was good at and loved.  Among students, he was often considered a favorite.  Among alumni, he was often considered an inspiration.  Many of his former pupils credit him for their present commitment to the Catholic faith. 

Being attracted to the life of prayer and the “peace and joy” that he found among the monks of Saint Bernard Abbey, Christopher Kuehler applied for the postulancy in 2008, at the conclusion of his second year on faculty at Saint Bernard.  He entered the novitiate on August 14, 2008, and received the religious name Anselm.  This name change proved difficult for some of the students, and in the initial months of his novitiate, they frequently referred to him as “Brother Mr. Kuehler.” He professed his simple vows on August 15 of the following year.  As a junior monk, Brother Anselm served as socius to the novices and community archivist.  He also resumed his teaching duties in the school.  In the fall of 2011, he briefly went away to complete studies for ordination at Saint John’s School of Theology, Collegeville, Minnesota.  But it was during this time that the first symptoms of what would come to be diagnosed as Alzheimer’s appeared.  After returning home to the abbey in order to receive the medical attention and and fraternal support he would need, Brother Anselm was accepted by the community for solemn profession in August of 2012.

He bore the news of his condition with heroic courage and acceptance, and even an occasional joke. The disease progressed quickly, but the faith and commitment which characterized his monastic resolve were extraordinary. During these years of declining health, Brother Anselm accompanied Brothers Augustine and Peter on their weekly community shopping trips to Walmart, and tried, longer than he was able, to participate in the common life of prayer and fraternity.  One of the hardest things for Brother Anselm to accept was that the disease had robbed him of the ability to do the work he loved the most: teaching.  As his mental proficiency weakened, many of his utterances involved teaching and classroom lecturing.  In the final year of his life, he required substantial assistance.  But he remained at the abbey, and his confreres, from the abbot to the novices, helped care for his daily needs, which became a significant element of community life.

Having received the last sacraments, Brother Anselm was called forth from this world at the age of fifty-five on Monday, January 25, 2016, the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul.  He died surrounded by his confreres and siblings.  The Funeral Mass was celebrated by Abbot Cletus on Friday, January 29, in the abbey church, which was filled not only with Brother Anselm’s confreres, family, and friends, but with many former and current students, a testament to his legacy as an educator.  

He is survived by his parents Hank and Carol, as well as his siblings David, Kathleen, Eric, John, and Joseph, and their families, including many nieces and nephews.

Brother Anselm was a selfless man of great integrity and genuine goodness.  His confreres recall his gentle wit and sweet, self-deprecating humor.  But one thing that Brother Anselm might have been wrong about was that his disease robbed him of his ability to be a teacher.  In fact, he became one of our most effective instructors: He taught our community how to follow Christ in the most profound of ways.  Through his suffering, and through our participation in it, he transformed our community into better, holier, more compassionate, more loving men.  

Although his monastic life was all too brief, it was undoubtedly one of the most fruitful ever lived at Saint Bernard.  For that gift, we are immensely grateful.

February 3, 1930 - April 17, 2018

Abbot Cletus and the monks of St. Bernard Abbey receive the news of the passing of our bishop emeritus with great sadness and offer our condolences to Bishop Baker and the priests of the Diocese of Birmingham.

Bishop Foley was ordained as a priest for the Archdiocese of Washington on May 26, 1956.  He was appointed by Pope John Paul II the Auxiliary Bishop of the Diocese of Richmond in Virginia on May 3, 1986, and consecrated on June 27, 1986.  Pope John Paul II later appointed Bishop Foley the third Bishop of Birmingham in Alabama on March 22, 1994.  He led the diocese until his retirement in May of 2005.

Yet, even in retirement, Bishop Foley remained very active in his priestly ministry in North Alabama until the final months of his life.  He died peacefully last night at the St. John Vianney Residence for Priests in Birmingham.  He was a dear friend of the abbey, and he will forever be remembered as a kind human being and a caring pastor of souls.

EXTRAORDINARY MEETING OF MONASTIC CHAPTER FOR THE ELECTION OF AN ABBOT

Dear friends, next week, the abbot president of the American Cassinese Congregation of Benedictine Monasteries, the Right Reverend Elias R. Lorenzo, OSB, will convene and preside over an extraordinary meeting of the monastic chapter (composed of all monks in final vows) of St. Bernard Abbey for the election of a new abbot.  In a Benedictine abbey, the office of the abbot is of singular importance, having the highest responsibility for all matters, both spiritual and temporal.

Over the last 128 years, since the first monks founded an abbey in Cullman, nine men have guided this monastic community and its various works of service to the Church, including our schools and countless parishes, ensuring a Benedictine presence in the Deep South that now spans three centuries:

Abbot Benedict Menges, OSB (1891-1904)

Abbot Boniface Seng, OSB (1939-1957)

Abbot Hilary Dreaper, OSB (1972-1987)
Abbot Victor Clark, OSB (1987-1995)

At 11:15 on Tuesday, July 23, the election will begin with a Mass solemnly invoking the Holy Spirit to guide the hearts of the monks in this most significant and sacred moment in St. Bernard’s history.  At this point, Abbot Cletus ceases to be the superior of St. Bernard and joins Abbot Victor as “abbot emeritus.”  Later that day, the chapter will convene for the first session in which candidates will be nominated.  That same evening, the first ballot of voting is expected to take place.  Unless a two-thirds majority is reached Tuesday night, voting will continue on Wednesday the 24th and potentially on Thursday the 25th.  For an abbot to be successfully elected on the first three ballots, a two-thirds majority is needed; afterwards, a simple majority of one more than half constitutes a successful election.  The new abbot fully assumes office immediately upon his acceptance of his election.  The election being confirmed by the abbot president, before the community the new abbot will make an oath of fidelity to the Church and be given the pectoral cross, a sign of the abbot holding the place of Christ in the community.  Normally, within three months of the election, the Mass of Abbatial Blessing takes place, at which the new abbot receives a special blessing to carry out his responsibilities and takes the liturgical vestments of miter and crozier.

Prior Leo, secretary of the abbatial election, and the monks of St. Bernard are most grateful for your prayers for each of us during this momentous time of discernment, as well as for the monk who is about to be chosen as the tenth abbot of St. Bernard and charged with the enormous task of guiding this “school of the Lord’s service” into its next chapter.

SAVE THE DATE: 
ABBATIAL BLESSING OF ABBOT MARCUS SET FOR OCTOBER 14

Friends, many of you have asked about what sort of formal ceremony there may be to mark the beginning of Abbot Marcus’s abbacy.

While an abbot and a bishop exercise similar roles of authority in the Church, and traditionally wear most of the same vestments, the office of abbot is only a juridical one, not a sacramental one like that of bishop (and priest and deacon).  That’s why abbots cannot ordain others, while bishops can.

Since Abbot Marcus does not advance to another sacramental order like a man does when he is made a bishop, there is no “ordination” of him as an abbot.  Nor, in our case, is there an “installation” of him as abbot since, according to the constitutions of our congregation and the proper law of the Benedictine Confederation and the Universal Church, Abbot Marcus fully became abbot of St. Bernard Abbey with all the rights, privileges, and responsibilities of a major religious superior of an institute of the pontifical right the moment his acceptance of his election was confirmed by the abbot president in the name of the Holy See, which was done in the election room just moments after the successful ballot had been announced.  Therefore, it’s improper to refer to him as “abbot-elect”; he is already the abbot in every since of the word!

However, there will be a special ceremony called an “abbatial blessing” (not abbatial “ordination” or “installation”).  Normally, this blessing of a new abbot (or a new abbess in the case of nuns) is given in the context of a festive Mass, celebrated with an abbey’s many friends, relatives, and supporters.  Like other things that the Church blesses, in this occasion God’s graces are implored for a particular purpose, namely for the new abbot to receive the strength, wisdom, and faith needed for his new responsibility of leading the monks and governing the abbey and its various works.

In this Mass of Abbatial Blessing, Abbot Marcus will receive the liturgical insignia of miter (the flame-shaped hat worn by abbots and bishops, signifying their role as teacher) and the crozier (the shepherd’s crook carried by abbots and bishops, signifying their pastoral role).  

The date has been set for Monday, October 14, 2019 (Columbus Day).

While there’s still a lot of planning to do, the monks wanted to give you the opportunity to mark your calendar as soon as possible, to “save the date,” and to plan to join us for this happy day in which we ask God’s blessing upon our new father in Christ.  The principle celebrant will be the Most Reverend Robert J. Baker, S.T.D., Bishop of Birmingham, and many other abbots are expected to attend the grand celebration.

APPOINTMENT OF NEW PRIOR

After consultation with the monastic community and prayerful consideration, the Right Reverend Marcus J. Voss, OSB, abbot of St. Bernard, has announced his appointment of the Very Reverend Francis M. Reque, OSB, as prior.

After the abbot, the prior (from the Latin, meaning “first”) ranks highest among the monks and is charged with oversight for all the day-to-day operations of the monastery.  In the absence of the abbot, the prior assumes the role of superior.

Prior Francis is a native of Minneapolis, Minnesota.  He came to St. Bernard in the early 90s, and professed monastic vows on March 21, 1995.  An avid reader with a degree in history from Augsburg University, he went on to study theology at St. Meinrad School of Theology, and was subsequently ordained to the priesthood in 2000.  He has held various positions and roles of responsibility at St. Bernard over the years, including serving as novice master; teaching Latin at St. Bernard Preparatory School and in the novitiate; and, most recently, assisting the diocesan clergy in their care for the pastoral needs of the people of the Diocese of Birmingham.

Prior Francis assumed the office of prior effective last Thursday, August 8, 2019.  He succeeds Brother Leo Borelli, OSB, who has served the monastic community faithfully and dutifully as prior for the last five years.

The Benedictine monks of Saint Bernard Abbey joyfully welcome Bishop Steven Raica, who was installed as the fifth bishop of the Diocese of Birmingham this Tuesday.  

Since the first Benedictines were sent to North Alabama in the 1870s to help the sole diocesan priest providing the sacramental and pastoral needs of Catholics in what’s now the entire territory of the Diocese of Birmingham, we have worked hard to build up the local Church as partners with the bishop and the diocesan priests, first of the Archdiocese of Mobile, and then the Diocese of Birmingham after its establishment in 1969.  We look forward to continuing this long heritage now with the fifth shepherd of the Church in North Alabama.

Abbot Marcus and the monks offer our sympathy upon the death of Saint Bernard College alumnus and longtime friend, the Most Reverend Oscar Lipscomb, archbishop emeritus of Mobile.  Following his philosophical studies at Saint Bernard, he studied theology in Rome and was ordained to the priesthood for the Diocese of Mobile-Birmingham on July 15, 1956.  He was appointed the eighth bishop – and first archbishop – of Mobile on July 29, 1980, by Pope Saint John Paul II.  In 2010, Archbishop Lipscomb was honored at the commencement ceremonies of Saint Bernard Preparatory School as a recipient of the Distinguished Alumnus Award (pictured here).  A native son of Mobile, Archbishop Lipscomb served the Church of South Alabama all of his priestly ministry, including 28 years as its archbishop.

It is a tradition that each priest has his own chalice. Every chalice has a story behind it and is dear to the priest to whom it belongs. Many priests get their chalices as a gift when they leave seminary, while others receive theirs from their parish or friends later on. Some priests may also inherit their chalices from other priests or family members. The chalice is usually engraved with the priest’s name and ordination date, and sometimes with a motto or a symbol of his patron saint.

The chalice is not just a vessel, but a sign of the priest’s identity and mission. It represents his participation in the sacrifice of Christ, who offered His blood for the salvation of the world. The chalice also reminds the priest of his call to serve God and His people with love and generosity, as he shares the precious gift of the Eucharist with them.

We congratulate our new priests Fr. Paschal and Fr. Pachomius and pray that they may always offer the holy sacrifice with reverence and devotion. May their chalices be a reminder of their commitment to serve God and His Church as faithful ministers of His word and sacrament.

Dear friends of St. Bernard abbey,

Today we celebrate a special feast of our holy father St. Benedict, the founder of Western monasticism and the patron saint of Europe! 🙏

You may wonder why we have two feast days for St. Benedict in the year. The answer is that the Church honors both his death and his translation. His death, or transitus, occurred on March 21, 547, and is celebrated by Benedictines as the primary feast day. His translation, or moving of his relics, occurred on July 11, 680, when his bones were transferred from Montecassino to Fleury in France to protect them from the Lombards. This date became the feast day for St. Benedict in the Universal Church.

St. Benedict was born in Italy around 480 and left the corruption of Rome to seek God in solitude. He founded several monasteries, including the famous Monte Cassino, where he wrote his Rule for monks. His Rule is based on the principles of prayer, work, simplicity, and hospitality, and has guided countless men and women to holiness for over 15 centuries.

St. Benedict died around 547, but his legacy lives on in the Benedictine family that spans the globe. He is also the patron saint of Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI, who chose his name as a sign of his admiration and devotion.

As we celebrate this great saint today, let us ask for his intercession to help us follow his motto: "Prefer nothing to the love of Christ." St. Benedict, pray for us!

Today we celebrate the feast day of our beloved Abbot Victor, who has been a faithful shepherd and a wise leader for our community for many years. Abbot Victor was named after St. Pope Victor I, the first African pope and a defender of orthodoxy and unity in the early Church. St. Pope Victor I was born in Africa in the second century and became the bishop of Rome around 189 C.E. He is known for his efforts to settle the controversy over the date of Easter, his condemnation of heresies, and his use of Latin as the official language of the Roman Church. He died a martyr around 199 C.E. 

Abbot Victor has followed the example of his patron saint in many ways. He guided our abbey through the challenging times of the 80s, when many religious vocations declined and secular influences increased. He also presided over the repayment of our government bond, which enabled us to improve our facilities and hospitality. He has always been a man of prayer, inspiring us to live out our Benedictine vows with joy and fidelity.

Abbot Victor is now suffering from dementia, which affects his memory and cognition. He is still a valued member of our community and we pray for him daily. He enjoys receiving visitors, especially when they bring cookies, which are his favorite treat. If you would like to visit him, please contact Joanna Bell, our Infirmary Supervisor, at jbell@stbernardabbey.com. We ask visitors to be respectful and gentle with him, as he may not remember you or your conversation. Please do not take it personally if he seems confused or forgetful. He is still a child of God and a brother in Christ.

We thank God for the gift of Abbot Victor and St. Pope Victor I, who have shown us how to serve God and His Church with courage and love. May they intercede for us and bless us with their prayers. Happy feast day, Abbot Victor!

Last Friday, we celebrated the feast day of Saint Leo the Great, one of the most important popes and theologians in the history of the Church. He was born in Tuscany around the year 400, and became a deacon in Rome, where he distinguished himself by his eloquence and wisdom. He was elected pope in 440, and faced many challenges and crises, such as the invasion of Attila the Hun, the heresy of Monophysitism, and the schism of the Eastern Church. He defended the faith with courage and clarity, and wrote many letters and sermons that are still studied and admired today. He is the first pope to be called “the Great”, and he is also a Doctor of the Church.

We also honored our own Brother Leo Borelli, OSB, who shares the name and the spirit of this great saint. Brother Leo has served as the Prior, Novice Master and is currently the Latin instructor at St. Bernard Preparatory School. He is a man of prayer, learning, and service, who inspires us by his example and his kindness. We thank God for his vocation and his presence among us.

Let us ask Saint Leo the Great to intercede for us, and to help us grow in love and holiness. Happy belated feast day!

It is with heavy hearts that Abbot Marcus and the monks of Saint Bernard Abbey announce the death of our confrere, Abbot Victor Joseph Clark, O.S.B.

A native of Cullman, Alabama, Abbot Victor professed vows as a Benedictine monk of St. Bernard Abbey on June 18, 1949, was ordained to the priesthood on June 5, 1954, and was elected the Eighth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey on May 22, 1987.  Spending his life in service of St. Bernard, he was beloved by many alumni and friends of the abbey from Alabama and beyond. Suffering from dementia for quite some time, Abbot Victor died in the St. Bernard Abbey Infirmary at 7:30 a.m. on Saturday, January 27, 2024, after a nightlong vigil with Abbot Marcus and the monks.

FUNERAL ARRANGEMENTS:

The monks will receive his body into the Abbey Church and celebrate Solemn Vespers of the Dead on Wednesday, January 31, at 5:00 p.m.

Visitation will be held until the Mass of Christian Burial.

The Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 3:00 p.m. on Thursday, February 1, with procession to the Abbey cemetery and interment following immediately.  Afterwards, all are invited to join Abbot Marcus and the monks for dinner in the St. Bernard Dining Hall.

St. Thomas Aquinas is a special inspiration for us at St. Bernard Abbey, where we strive to seek God and glorify him in all things. We thank God for the gift of St. Thomas Aquinas and Brother Thomas Jones, and we ask for their intercession for our community and our school. May we all follow their example of seeking the truth and serving the Lord with our minds and hearts. Amen.

OBITUARY FOR ABBOT VICTOR CLARK

The Right Reverend Victor Joseph Clark, O.S.B.

A.D. 1930 – 2024

It is with heavy hearts that Abbot Marcus Voss, O.S.B., and the Monks of St. Bernard Abbey announce the death of their confrere, The Right Reverend Victor Joseph Clark, O.S.B., Eighth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey, who went to God on January 27, 2024.

Baptized Joseph Jude Clark, Abbot Victor was born in Cullman, Alabama on January 7, 1930, the eighth of nine children, to Rene Marcus Clark and Anna Marie Schwann.  Raised in Cullman, Abbot Victor grew up in the “shadow of St. Bernard,” as he liked to say, attending Sacred Heart Elementary School.  After graduating from grammar school in 1943, Abbot Victor took a summer job delivering groceries at White Star Market in Cullman.  During that summer, our Fr. Philip Niedermeier called him into the rectory of Sacred Heart Parish Church and advised Abbot Victor to enter the seminary at St. Bernard.  That he did, beginning his studies in our high-school seminary the following September at the age of 13.  In 1948 he entered the novitiate at St. Bernard Abbey, receiving the religious name “Victor.”  He professed Simple Vows on June 18, 1949 and Solemn Vows in 1952.  Meanwhile his older sister, Frances, entered Sacred Heart Convent in Cullman, receiving the name Sr. Mary Jude, after the middle name of her Benedictine brother.

During his early years in vows, Abbot Victor studied at our college and at St. Benedict’s College in Atchison, Kansas, earning a Bachelor of Science degree in Biology.  He then studied Theology at St. Bernard, after which he was ordained to the Priesthood on June 5, 1954 by the Bishop of Mobile, Bishop T. J. Toolen, at Sacred Heart Church in Cullman.  Abbot Victor celebrated his Solemn Mass of Thanksgiving the next day, the Solemnity of Pentecost, with his nephew of ten years, Marcus Voss, serving at his First Mass.  Little did those present know that his nephew would one day follow him as monk, priest, and Abbot of St. Bernard!

Completing his Master of Science degree in Botany in 1956 from the Alabama Polytechnic Institute (now Auburn University), Abbot Victor took on increasing responsibility in our abbey and schools.  Through the years, he served as Prefect in the High School Seminary, the Major Seminary, as well as in many dormitories on the campus.  He was appointed Dean of Students in 1965, all the while teaching Biology in our high school and college from 1952 to 1979.  In the summer he supplied pastoral service to many parishes in the South.  In 1976 Abbot Victor was appointed Procurator of the Abbey, a position which he held until his appointment as Pastor of St. Bartholomew Catholic Church, Elberta, Alabama, in 1982.  He was recalled to St. Bernard to serve as Prior of the monastery in 1986.  He held this position for only a year, after which time he was elected the Eighth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey.

Holding the Office of Abbot for eight years, Abbot Victor’s abbacy was defined by his quiet strength.  After the 1988 tornadoes which devastated Cullman and did significant damage to our campus, Abbot Victor oversaw the restoration of the Administration Building to its historic appearance, an outward expression of his deep appreciation for St. Bernard’s history and its patrimony.  He was thus well suited to preside over the Centennial Jubilee of the Abbey in 1991.  It was for this occasion that he researched, prepared, and published a large format booklet of the hundred-year history of St. Bernard Abbey.

A fine athlete and excellent baseball player, Abbot Victor had a lifelong appreciation for sports.  Thus, during his abbacy, he made preparations for our new gymnasium to be built, the Fasi-Richard Athletic Center.  Though this project was finished after his reign, he laid the groundwork for the future project.

After resigning from the Office of Abbot at the age of 65, he assumed responsibility as pastor animarum at St. Michael Catholic Church, St. Florian, Alabama, for the next thirteen years.  Returning home to the Abbey at the age of 78, Abbot Victor often could be found in the Abbey Church.  A man of deep prayer and profound quiet, he was a sought after confessor by many of the brethren and guests alike.  Always a man of physical activity, Abbot Victor continued his monastic labora even as he aged.  In the afternoons, he could be seen mowing grass and working on other outdoor projects.

Suffering from dementia for many years, Abbot Victor’s mind and body increasingly declined.  In 2020, at the age of 90, he entered the monastic infirmary where he could receive more personalized care.  Cared for by monks and coworkers alike, his strong and independent spirit remained with him even as his body and mind failed.  As he gradually lost his faculties, one thing remained: his deep and abiding faith in God.  In times of distress, he would often call upon the name of Jesus.  And in his dying days, when he was beyond the point of conversation, he was heard repeating, “Hear my voice.  Hear my prayer.  Save my soul.”  On the early morning hours of Saturday, January 27, Abbot Marcus and the monks kept vigil at Abbot Victor’s bedside.  Having received the Anointing of the Sick and the Apostolic Pardon, Abbot Victor died peacefully at 7:30 a.m. that morning.  At the time of his death, he was the senior monk and priest of our house, celebrating his seventieth jubilee of priestly ordination.

Abbot Victor’s life was one marked by dedication to God and faithful service to St. Bernard.  From the time he was a young monk, he shouldered significant responsibility for the community.  Firm but kind, Abbot Victor was a humble man who did not readily complain or shirk responsibility.  Instead, he gave himself to God and to this place of St. Bernard which he loved so much.

Rt. Rev. Marcus J. Voss, O.S.B. and Community
St. Bernard Abbey
Cullman, Alabama

Happy feast day of St. John Bosco, the patron saint of editors, publishers, youth, apprentices, and magicians! St. John Bosco was a 19th century Italian priest who reached out to young people to remedy their lack of education, opportunities, and faith. He founded the Salesian order, which continues his mission of serving the poor and needy children of the world. He also wrote many books and pamphlets, and used his skills as a magician to attract and entertain his audience.

St. John Bosco is a special inspiration for us at St. Bernard Abbey, where we strive to follow his example of joy, kindness, and trust in God's providence. We are blessed to have among us Fr. John O'Donnell, who shares the name and the zeal of the Gentle Father of the Young. Fr. John is a Philadelphia native, who attended St. Bernard during its days as a college, and has been a monk at the Abbey since the 1980s. He has served as the manager of the Ave Maria Grotto, the athletic director for St. Bernard Prep School, the associate pastor of Sacred Heart of Jesus Church in Cullman, and the chaplain of the Cullman County Sheriff's Office. 

We thank God for the gift of St. John Bosco and Fr. John O'Donnell, and we ask for their intercession for our community and our school. May we all follow their motto: "Give me souls, take away the rest." Amen.

On Ash Wednesday, the call is for repentance and inward turning. But in a world defined by noise, distraction, and relentless self-promotion, how can we find that interior space? Here's where St. Benedict's wisdom feels radically countercultural. In this reflection, explore we explore the Benedictine idea of 'listening with the ear of the heart.' It's an invitation to silence the inner clamor and actively embrace the world around us – the whispers of creation, and the often-unheard cries of the suffering. Let's step into a different rhythm this Lent.

Lent isn't about escapism; it's about facing the darkest corners of ourselves and our world.  St. Benedict understood the unseen forces at play in our lives. This reflection explores his concept of spiritual warfare and provides tools to combat the very real enemies of pride, despair, and temptation.

Remember when Rome fell and our culture was nearly lost? Benedictine monks became its safekeepers. Today, the battle for beauty, wisdom, and goodness continues – and, like our spiritual ancestors, we can choose to be guardians of the light. This Lent, let's explore how to cultivate a discerning heart, enrich our own lives, and fight back against the darkness.

In our divisive world, extending welcome to 'the other' can feel like an act of defiance. In Lent, this spirit of resistance to cynicism is more essential than ever.  Learn how Benedictine hospitality invites us to be radically generous like Christ, offering a countercultural witness of love.

The Psalms are filled with themes of repentance, longing, and hope – perfect for Lenten reflection. The Benedictine tradition of the Liturgy of the Hours weaves these ancient poems into a daily framework of prayer. Could this practice deepen your Lenten experience?

Lent invites us to strip away distractions and focus on what truly matters. The Benedictine concept of detachment offers a powerful path for this season. It's not about coldness or indifference, but about freeing ourselves from unhealthy attachments to rediscover a deeper love for God and others. Intrigued? Explore the Benedictine path to detachment and discover spiritual freedom.

Do you long for a deeper connection with God? To hear His voice more clearly in the challenges and joys of life? This Lent, explore the Benedictine practice of lectio divina. Let Scripture become a living, transformative force within you.

Yesterday marked the feast day of St. Pachomius, a remarkable figure in early Christian monasticism. Born in Egypt around 290 AD, Pachomius is credited with establishing the first organized monastic communities, where monks lived and worked together under a shared rule. His vision emphasized a balance of prayer, work, and communal living, shaping the monastic tradition for centuries to come.

His legacy serves as a beacon of hope, reminding us of the power of faith and the courage to stand for what is right.

Thrilled to share some exciting news from St. Bernard Abbey! 🙏 As we joyfully gear up to move back into our beautifully renovated monastery, we at St. Bernard Abbey are doubly pleased to be making the move with our three newly minted novices! It truly feels like springtime in every way, a time of fresh beginnings and spiritual renewal. 

Last Friday at Vespers, Postulant Nathan Jackson, Postulant Alex Tucker, and Postulant Sean Ray reached a significant milestone in their journey as they were received into the novitiate!
This step follows an initial period called the postulancy, which is a time for men discerning a monastic vocation to live within the community and experience the monastic life more directly while still retaining their baptismal names.

The novitiate is the next stage, a dedicated year of more intensive formation. During this time, the novices deepen their understanding of the Benedictine way of life, engage in study of the Rule of St. Benedict and monastic practices, and further discern God's call. It's a crucial period of learning and growth, solidifying their commitment to our community.

At the beginning of the novitiate, the men are given religious names. This tradition symbolizes a new beginning in Christ and a deeper consecration to God. It signifies a leaving behind of their former identity in the world to embrace a new life dedicated to prayer and service within the monastic community.

Our postulants have received these new names:
Br. Raphael (left), after the Archangel Raphael: One of the seven archangels who is known as a healer and helper in the Bible.

Br. Anthony (middle), after Saint Anthony of the Desert: Considered the father of Christian monasticism, he lived a life of solitude and prayer in the Egyptian desert.

Br. Damien (right), after Saint Damien of Molokai: A priest who ministered to people with leprosy in Hawaii and is known for his compassionate service and sacrifice.

Let us continue to pray for Br. Damien, Br. Anthony, and Br. Raphael during this important year of their novitiate, that they may be filled with the grace and wisdom to follow Christ faithfully in the Benedictine tradition.

Abbot Marcus and the Monks of St. Bernard Abbey, in union with the whole Church, express sorrow at the death of our Holy Father Pope Francis, the Roman Pontiff.

"May the angels lead him into paradise; at his arrival, may the martyrs receive him and lead him into the holy city Jerusalem. May choir of angels receive him and with Lazarus, who was once a poor man, may you have eternal rest."

Today, we rejoice in the Easter Octave, celebrating the Resurrection of Christ, which takes liturgical precedence over all other feasts, including the Feast of St. Mark. In honor of St. Mark the Evangelist, we also remember Abbot Marcus J. Voss, O.S.B.. As the Tenth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey, Abbot Marcus has served 60 years with unwavering faith and leadership in Cullman.

Born in 1943 and raised at Sacred Heart Parish, Abbot Marcus excelled in athletics and academics before answering his monastic calling. His athletic ability and extensive contributions as a school administrator earned him a place in the Cullman County Sports Hall of Fame in 2008. A graduate of St. Bernard, St. Bede Abbey, and St. Louis University, he holds a Master of Divinity and a master’s in Christian spirituality. Ordained in 1971, he has served as teacher, headmaster, president, and Chairman of St. Bernard Preparatory School, which he helped re-establish in 1984. 

Happy Feast Day Abbot Marcus!

Today, we continue to rejoice in the Easter Octave, celebrating the Resurrection of Christ, which takes liturgical precedence over all other feasts. In the spirit of this sacred time, we honor Abbot Cletus D. Meagher, O.S.B., the Ninth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey, who served with profound faith and leadership in Cullman.

Born in 1944 in Cleveland, Tennessee, Abbot Cletus attended St. Bernard for high school and college, entering monastic life in 1964. Professing simple vows in 1965, he studied theology at St. Bede Abbey and the University of St. Louis, and was ordained a priest in 1971. Before his election as abbot in 1995, he served in diverse roles, including prior, novice master, procurator, farm manager, and pastor of Sacred Heart Church. Leading the abbey for nearly a quarter century until his retirement in 2019, he guided the community with wisdom and gratitude, fostering its spiritual and apostolic missions.

Happy feast day, Abbot Cletus!

Today we celebrate the feast of St. Joseph the Worker. We also honor our own Br. Joseph, who shares his name and his spirit of service with this great saint. 

“Work contains goodness within itself, creates harmony between things – beauty, goodness – and involves every part of the person. This is man’s first vocation: work. This gives dignity to mankind. Dignity makes us similar to God.” - Pope Francis

Yesterday, we celebrated the Feast Day of St. Damien of Molokai, whose selfless devotion to the lepers of Molokai inspires us to live with compassion and service. His legacy of caring for the marginalized continues to guide our community at St. Bernard Abbey.

We also give thanks for our newly minted novice, Br. Damien (pictured far right), whose name honors this compassionate saint's legacy. On March 21st, Br. Damien, alongside Br. Anthony (standing beside him) and Br. Raphael (far left), began their monastic journey as novices. Their commitment to a life of prayer and service is a blessing to our abbey and a living echo of St. Damien’s mission.

We also extend our prayers and gratitude to all mothers on this Mother’s Day, whose love and sacrifice reflect God’s care. Please join us in praying for Br. Damien, Br. Anthony, and Br. Raphael as they grow in faith, and for all mothers who nurture our world. May St. Damien of Molokai and the Blessed Virgin Mary guide them all. 🙏

Today marks the feast day of St. Pachomius, a remarkable figure in early Christian monasticism. Born in Egypt around 290 AD, Pachomius is credited with establishing the first organized monastic communities, where monks lived and worked together under a shared rule. His vision emphasized a balance of prayer, work, and communal living, shaping the monastic tradition for centuries to come. 

In the spirit of St. Pachomius, we also celebrate our own Fr. Pachomius, a beloved member of the St. Bernard monastic community. Born in Cuba, Fr. Pachomius discovered his monastic calling while working in Colombia. Since arriving at St. Bernard Abbey in 2014, he has embraced our community's values of prayer, work, and fellowship. As Associate Pastor of St. Francis Catholic Church in Birmingham, Fr. Pachomius exemplifies the monastic spirit through his dedication to God and service to others. We are grateful for his presence in our community and wish him continued blessings on his spiritual journey.

Today, we honor St. Brendan the Navigator, a 6th-century Irish monk renowned for his legendary voyages across the Atlantic. While the historical details are shrouded in myth and folklore, St. Brendan's unwavering faith and adventurous spirit continue to inspire. His quest for the "Isle of the Blessed" symbolizes the Christian journey towards God, a pilgrimage filled with both challenges and divine encounters. May St. Brendan's courage and trust in God's providence guide us on our own spiritual journeys.

In the spirit of exploration and hospitality, we also celebrate our own Brother Brendan Seipel, O.S.B., who hails from New Albany, Indiana. Since professing his vows in 2004, Br. Brendan has wholeheartedly embraced the monastic life at St. Bernard Abbey. Currently stewarding our abbey's farm, he tends to the land with care and dedication, embodying the Benedictine values of work and self-sufficiency.  We are grateful for Br. Brendan's dedication to fostering a spirit of welcome and fellowship within our monastic family. May God continue to bless him in his ministry and monastic journey.

Today we celebrate the feast day of St. Paschal Baylon, the patron saint of Eucharistic Congresses and Associations. St. Paschal's life, marked by simplicity, humility, and an unwavering love for the Eucharist, serves as a shining beacon of faith and devotion.

In the same spirit of youthful energy and dedication, we also celebrate our own Fr. Paschal. Like his namesake, Fr. Paschal radiates a vibrant light within our monastery. His exceptional talents, honed by the Nashville Dominican Sisters at St. Rose Academy, have proven invaluable to our community. From his pivotal role in our recent fundraising efforts to his ongoing service as our Director of Development, Fr. Paschal's contributions have been nothing short of extraordinary. Ordained just last June, Fr. Paschal's journey is only beginning, yet he has already left an indelible mark on our monastery. His youthful enthusiasm, coupled with his deep-rooted faith, inspires us all. As we celebrate St. Paschal Baylon today, we also pray that he intercedes for our own Fr. Paschal, guiding and strengthening him in his vocation.

Today, we celebrate St. Bede, a remarkable scholar, historian, and monk who lived in 8th-century England. Known for his immense contributions to literature, history, and theology, St. Bede is the patron of scholars, historians, and English people. His most famous work, "Ecclesiastical History of the English People," remains a cornerstone of English history. He's also known for his deep devotion to learning, his prolific writing, and his unwavering faith.

Here at St. Bernard Abbey, we have a special connection to St. Bede through our very own Fr. Bede Marcy, O.S.B. Fr. Bede, hailing from Biloxi, Mississippi, is our beloved dining hall manager and a dedicated theology instructor at St. Bernard Prep. He professed his vows on March 21, 2002, and was ordained a priest on May 2, 2009. We're grateful for Fr. Bede's service and his embodiment of St. Bede's spirit of intellectual curiosity and faithful dedication.

Join us in honoring St. Bede today, and say a prayer for Fr. Bede and all who carry on the saint's legacy of wisdom and faith.

Join us today as we celebrate the Feast Day of St. Charles Lwanga. A young Ugandan page in the royal court, St. Charles courageously defended his faith and the purity of the young men under his care when King Mwanga II demanded they renounce their Christian beliefs. Their refusal led to their horrific martyrdom, with St. Charles being burned alive in a furnace. His firey faith in the face of unimaginable suffering serves as an inspiration to all. Today, St. Charles Lwanga is the patron saint of African Catholic Youth Action, converts, and those facing persecution for their beliefs. His legacy serves as a beacon of hope, reminding us of the power of faith and the courage to stand for what is right.

Our own Br. Charles Manning, a pillar of our community, shares a deep connection with the spirit of St. Charles Lwanga. A devoted educator, Br. Charles has dedicated his life to nurturing young minds at St. Bernard Prep School, echoing St. Charles's unwavering commitment to youth. With a heart full of faith and a passion for learning, Br. Charles embodies the values that St. Charles Lwanga championed. On this Feast Day, we honor both St. Charles Lwanga and Br. Charles Manning, two men whose lives exemplify the transformative power of faith, education, and unwavering devotion to God and community.

Happy feast day to our Brother Irenaeus Ceballos, O.S.B., and to his heavenly patron, St. Irenaeus! 

Today we celebrate the life and legacy of St. Irenaeus, the bishop of Lyon, apologist, and leading Christian theologian of the 2nd century, who defended the faith against the Gnostics and other heretics and helped establish the canon of the four Gospels. As the patron of apologists and theologians, St. Irenaeus is a model of orthodoxy and unity.

We also honor Brother Irenaeus Ceballos, O.S.B., a native of Buenos Aires, Colombia, who has lived in the United States for over 28 years and became a U.S. citizen on November 15, 2015. With a bachelor’s degree in Philosophy from St. John Vianney College in Miami, Brother Irenaeus spent time as a seminarian for the Palm Beach Diocese and two and a half years at St. Leo Abbey before entering the postulancy at St. Bernard Abbey in January 2013. He professed his vows as a Benedictine on February 12, 2014, and has since served diligently in groundskeeping and maintenance, contributing to the abbey through painting, general maintenance, and campus upkeep.

Let us pray for St. Irenaeus’ intercession to bless Brother Irenaeus and all of us, guiding us in faith and unity.

Yesterday was the feast day of Fr. Joel Martin, O.S.B., the dean of St. Bernard and the vocation director of St. Bernard Abbey. Fr. Joel is a native of Fitzgerald, Georgia where he attended public schools, then graduated from Emory University in 1972. After earning M.A. and M.Div. degrees from St. Meinrad School of Theology he taught at St. Bernard Prep from 1991-1995. Then he was made Headmaster of the School and served in that position over fifteen years, being made President in 2013. He also serves as a Vocation Director and Choirmaster of St. Bernard Abbey. 

Fr. Joel shares his name with the prophet Joel, who lived in Judah around the 9th century BC and wrote the book of Joel in the Bible. The prophet Joel warned the people of Judah about a coming locust plague and a day of judgment, but also promised God’s mercy and restoration for those who repent and call on his name. The prophet Joel also foretold the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on all people, which was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost.

Let us thank God for the gift of Fr. Joel Martin and the prophet Joel, and ask for their intercession for our community and our world. May they inspire us to seek God and glorify him in all things.

Revered as the patron saint of travelers and motorists, St. Christopher's intercession is sought for protection against sudden death and toothaches. Legend tells us he once carried a child who revealed himself to be Christ.  St. Christopher's name, meaning "Christ-bearer," reminds us to carry Christ to others through our actions and words.

Br. Christopher embodies this spirit perfectly. Today we celebrate the Feast of St. Dominic, the founder of the Dominican Order. Renowned for his intellect and spirituality, St. Dominic is deeply connected to the Rosary devotion, which he popularized as a tool for contemplation and conversion. Interestingly, he is also the patron saint of astronomers. Legend has it that a star shone from his chest at baptism, a celestial sign interpreted as a divine omen. This heavenly association, combined with his intellectual pursuits, led to this unique patronage.

As we celebrate St. Dominic, we also rejoice in the life of our own Father Dominic Lee. From his homeschooling days under St. Peter’s Academy to his journey through monastic life, Father Dominic has dedicated his life to God's service. His sharp intellect, evident in his degrees in mathematics and philosophy, is matched only by his deep spirituality. We are truly blessed to have him as a priest, and we pray for his continued success as a teacher at St. Bernard Preparatory School. Happy Feast Day, Father Dominic!

Today we are celebrating the feast day of St. Augustine, patron saint of our dear Br. Augustine! A newly professed monk and former Navy submariner, Br. Augustine serves as Assistant Development Director. As the son of an Air Force officer, he was born in Pittsburgh, PA, and grew up in Dayton, OH, San Angelo, TX, Azores, Portugal, and Wichita Falls, TX. He has also lived in Hungary, Spain, and Hawaii.

St. Augustine was one of the greatest Christian thinkers and writers of all time. He was born in 354 in Algeria and converted to Christianity after a long and restless search for truth. He became the bishop of Hippo and wrote many influential works, such as Confessions and The City of God. He is also known for his doctrines of original sin, grace, and predestination. He died in 430 during the siege of Hippo by the Vandals. St. Augustine’s life and writings inspire us to seek God with all our heart, mind, and soul, and to love our neighbor as ourselves. He is the patron saint of brewers, printers, theologians, sore eyes, and many cities around the world. Let us ask for his intercession today and always.
St. Augustine, pray for us!

Today is the feast day of Pope St. Linus, the second bishop of Rome and a martyr of the early church. He is mentioned in the New Testament by St. Paul in 2 Timothy 4:21. He was entrusted with the office of the episcopate by the apostles Peter and Paul, and he ruled the church from about 67 to 76 or 79. He is among the martyrs named in the canon of the mass and his relics are venerated in several churches.

We are also celebrating one of our own monks, Fr. Linus Klucsarits, O.S.B. He enjoys gardening, baseball, and running. He is a native of Allentown, Pennsylvania.

We ask for the intercession of Pope St. Linus, who followed Christ faithfully and served his church with love and dedication. May he inspire us to live out our baptismal call to holiness and mission. We also thank God for the gift of Fr. Linus, who enriches our community with his talents and his joy. Happy feast day!

Today, we celebrate the feast of the archangels, Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, who are God’s faithful messengers and powerful protectors. We also celebrate with joy and gratitude our brothers, Br. Raphael Ray (left) and Br. Michael Gregerson (right). 

The archangels are honored in the Scriptures and in the tradition of the Church as the special agents of God’s plan of salvation. They announce God’s word, defend God’s people, and heal God’s creation. Happy feast day, Br. Thomas! 
St. Thomas Aquinas is the patron saint of students, scholars, and philosophers. He was a brilliant theologian and a master of the harmony between faith and reason. He wrote many works, including the Summa Theologica, which is considered one of the greatest achievements of Christian thought. He also composed beautiful hymns, such as the Adoro Te Devote and the Pange Lingua Gloriosi.
Our Brother Thomas Jones shares the name and the love of learning of the Angelic Doctor. He is our librarian and the coach of the St. Bernard Prep's trivia bowl team. He is always ready to help students and guests with their research and reading needs, and to challenge them with his vast knowledge of various subjects. He is also a humble and joyful monk, who lives out the Benedictine motto of prayer and work.

Today we celebrate Fr. John O'Donnell and the feast day of St. John Bosco, the patron saint of editors, publishers, youth, apprentices, and magicians! 

St. John Bosco was a 19th century Italian priest who reached out to young people to remedy their lack of education, opportunities, and faith. He founded the Salesian order, which continues his mission of serving the poor and needy children of the world. He also wrote many books and pamphlets, and used his skills as a magician to attract and entertain his audience.

St. John Bosco is a special inspiration for us at St. Bernard Abbey, where we strive to follow his example of joy, kindness, and trust in God's providence. We are blessed to have among us Fr. John is a Philadelphia native, who attended St. Bernard during its days as a college, and has been a monk at the Abbey since the 1980s. He has served as the manager of the Ave Maria Grotto, the athletic director for St. Bernard Prep School, the associate pastor of Sacred Heart of Jesus Church in Cullman, and the chaplain of the Cullman County Sheriff's Office. 

We thank God for the gift of St. John Bosco and Fr. John O'Donnell, and we ask for their intercession for our community and our school. May we all follow their motto: "Give me souls, take away the rest." Amen.

Last Saturday’s celebration of the Transitus of St. Benedict was a day of deep joy and gratitude for our monastery.

In the course of the liturgy, three postulants were clothed in the holy habit and entered the novitiate, while two novices made their next step, professing temporary vows and entering the juniorate.

In our way of life, a man first spends six months as a postulant, learning the rhythms of prayer and community. He then receives the habit and begins a one-year novitiate, a more intense period of formation in the Rule of St. Benedict. After this, he may profess vows and enter the juniorate, a three-year period of continued formation before solemn profession.

With the reception of the habit, the new novices also receive new names:

Austin Smith is now Br. Nov. Nicholas (after St. Nicholas of Myra, feast day December 6)
Timothy Boland is now Br. Nov. Boniface (Apostle to Germany, feast day June 5)
Michael Maddox is now Br. Nov. Gabriel (after the Archangel, feast day September 29)

With this, the monastery now has all three archangels represented: Br. Michael, Br. Gabriel, and Br. Raphael.

Please keep these brothers in prayer as they begin this new stage of monastic life.

Today, as we celebrate the feast day of St. Mark the Evangelist—author of the earliest Gospel, companion of St. Peter, and a man whose writing moves with urgency, clarity, and vivid action—we give thanks for his witness to Christ. Tradition holds that Mark faithfully handed on what he received from Peter, preserving for the Church a Gospel that pulses with immediacy: Christ healing, teaching, suffering, and triumphing. Mark reminds us that discipleship is not abstract, but lived—often quickly, courageously, and at a cost.

In that same spirit, we also remember Abbot Marcus J. Voss, O.S.B. Abbot Marcus has served 60 years with unwavering faith and leadership in Cullman. Born in 1943 and raised at Sacred Heart Parish, Abbot Marcus excelled in athletics and academics before answering his monastic calling. His athletic ability and extensive contributions as a school administrator earned him a place in the Cullman County Sports Hall of Fame in 2008. A graduate of St. Bernard, St. Bede Abbey, and St. Louis University, he holds a Master of Divinity and a master’s in Christian spirituality. Ordained in 1971, he has served as teacher, headmaster, president, and Chairman of St. Bernard Preparatory School, which he helped re-establish in 1984. He also served as the 10th abbot of St. Bernard.
Happy Feast Day, Abbot Marcus!

Because today is Sunday, the Church celebrates the Lord’s Day—the weekly commemoration of the Resurrection—which always takes precedence over the memorials of saints. For that reason, the feast of St. Cletus (Anacletus), one of the early successors of St. Peter, is not observed liturgically this year. Still, we pause to remember him: a martyr and third Bishop of Rome who helped guide the young Church in its fragile beginnings, faithfully handing on the apostolic tradition.

In that spirit, we honor Abbot Cletus D. Meagher, O.S.B., the Ninth Abbot of St. Bernard Abbey, who served with profound faith and leadership in Cullman. Born in 1944 in Cleveland, Tennessee, Abbot Cletus attended St. Bernard for high school and college, entering monastic life in 1964. Professing simple vows in 1965, he studied theology at St. Bede Abbey and the University of St. Louis, and was ordained a priest in 1971. Before his election as abbot in 1995, he served in diverse roles, including prior, novice master, procurator, farm manager, and pastor of Sacred Heart Church. Leading the abbey for nearly a quarter century until his retirement in 2019, he guided the community with wisdom and gratitude, fostering its spiritual and apostolic missions.

We give thanks for Abbot Cletus and commend him to the Lord.

Today we celebrate the feast of St. Joseph the Worker. We also honor our own Br. Joseph, who shares his name and his spirit of service with this great saint. 

“Work contains goodness within itself, creates harmony between things – beauty, goodness – and involves every part of the person. This is man’s first vocation: work. This gives dignity to mankind. Dignity makes us similar to God.” - Pope Francis

Although Saint Damien of Molokai's feast day fell on a Sunday this year — displacing the official memorial in the liturgy — we joyfully honor his story and life. The Belgian priest who stepped ashore at Kalaupapa in 1873 and never left, spending himself entirely for the abandoned and dying, is well worth a belated celebration.

We also wish to honor our own Brother Damien Jackson, pictured here second from the right, standing next to Fr. Joel. Named for the Apostle of the Lepers, Brother Damien is growing daily in the life he has consecrated to God. May his patron's radical, unhesitating charity be a constant companion to him. 

We also extend love and gratitude to all mothers — especially those of our brothers — whose self-giving first showed them what they are now practicing.  🙏

Today marks the feast day of St. Pachomius, a remarkable figure in early Christian monasticism. Born in Egypt around 290 AD, Pachomius is credited with establishing the first organized monastic communities, where monks lived and worked together under a shared rule. His vision emphasized a balance of prayer, work, and communal living, shaping the monastic tradition for centuries to come. 

In the spirit of St. Pachomius, we also celebrate our own Fr. Pachomius, a beloved member of the St. Bernard monastic community. Born in Cuba, Fr. Pachomius discovered his monastic calling while working in Colombia. Since arriving at St. Bernard Abbey in 2014, he has embraced our community's values of prayer, work, and fellowship. As Associate Pastor of St. Francis Catholic Church in Birmingham, Fr. Pachomius exemplifies the monastic spirit through his dedication to God and service to others. We are grateful for his presence in our community and wish him continued blessings on his spiritual journey.

Today, we honor St. Brendan the Navigator, a 6th-century Irish monk renowned for his legendary voyages across the Atlantic. While the historical details are shrouded in myth and folklore, St. Brendan's unwavering faith and adventurous spirit continue to inspire. His quest for the "Isle of the Blessed" symbolizes the Christian journey towards God, a pilgrimage filled with both challenges and divine encounters. May St. Brendan's courage and trust in God's providence guide us on our own spiritual journeys.

In the spirit of exploration and hospitality, we also celebrate our own Brother Brendan Seipel, O.S.B., who hails from New Albany, Indiana. Since professing his vows in 2004, Br. Brendan has wholeheartedly embraced the monastic life at St. Bernard Abbey. Currently stewarding our abbey's farm, he tends to the land with care and dedication, embodying the Benedictine values of work and self-sufficiency.  We are grateful for Br. Brendan's dedication to fostering a spirit of welcome and fellowship within our monastic family. May God continue to bless him in his ministry and monastic journey.

Today is Sunday, so the feast of St. Paschal Baylon is not liturgically observed. Still, we remember him and our own Fr. Paschal.

St. Paschal Baylon, patron of Eucharistic Congresses and Associations, stands out for his simplicity, humility, and single-minded devotion to the Blessed Sacrament. In the same spirit, Fr. Paschal brings real energy and competence to our community. Trained by the Nashville Dominican Sisters at St. Rose Academy, he has already made a strong contribution through the recent fundraising efforts and in his role as Director of Development. 

As we recall St. Paschal Baylon, it is fitting to ask his intercession for Fr. Paschal—that the same Eucharistic love that shaped the saint may strengthen the priest in his vocation.

Today, we celebrate St. Bede, a remarkable scholar, historian, and monk who lived in 8th-century England. Known for his immense contributions to literature, history, and theology, St. Bede is the patron of scholars, historians, and English people. His most famous work, "Ecclesiastical History of the English People," remains a cornerstone of English history. He's also known for his deep devotion to learning, his prolific writing, and his unwavering faith.

Here at St. Bernard Abbey, we have a special connection to St. Bede through our very own Fr. Bede Marcy, O.S.B. Fr. Bede, hailing from Biloxi, Mississippi, is our beloved dining hall manager and a dedicated theology instructor at St. Bernard Prep. He professed his vows on March 21, 2002, and was ordained a priest on May 2, 2009. We're grateful for Fr. Bede's service and his embodiment of St. Bede's spirit of intellectual curiosity and faithful dedication.

Join us in honoring St. Bede today, and say a prayer for Fr. Bede and all who carry on the saint's legacy of wisdom and faith.

Join us today as we celebrate the Feast Day of St. Charles Lwanga. A young Ugandan page in the royal court, St. Charles courageously defended his faith and the purity of the young men under his care when King Mwanga II demanded they renounce their Christian beliefs. Their refusal led to their horrific martyrdom, with St. Charles being burned alive in a furnace. His firey faith in the face of unimaginable suffering serves as an inspiration to all. Today, St. Charles Lwanga is the patron saint of African Catholic Youth Action, converts, and those facing persecution for their beliefs. His legacy serves as a beacon of hope, reminding us of the power of faith and the courage to stand for what is right.

Our own Br. Charles Manning, a pillar of our community, shares a deep connection with the spirit of St. Charles Lwanga. A devoted educator, Br. Charles has dedicated his life to nurturing young minds at St. Bernard Prep School, echoing St. Charles's unwavering commitment to youth. With a heart full of faith and a passion for learning, Br. Charles embodies the values that St. Charles Lwanga championed. On this Feast Day, we honor both St. Charles Lwanga and Br. Charles Manning, two men whose lives exemplify the transformative power of faith, education, and unwavering devotion to God and community.

Today the Church honors Saint Boniface (c. 675–754), the English Benedictine monk known as the Apostle of Germany. Born Winfrid in Wessex, he answered a papal commission to evangelize the pagan Germanic peoples, boldly felling the sacred oak of the thunder-god Donar to demonstrate the power of the one true God, founding monasteries, organizing the Church across Germany, and ultimately dying a martyr's death on this day in 754 — struck down by pagan Frisians with the Scriptures open in his hands. A monk to the end, faithful and fearless. 

We're proud to share his feast day with our own Brother Boniface Boland, O.S.B., who entered the novitiate here at Saint Bernard Abbey on the Solemnity of the Transitus of Saint Benedict this past March. May his heavenly patron intercede for him as he continues his own Benedictine journey of prayer and conversion. Happy feast day, Brother Boniface! Ad multos annos! 🙏
